claim: In the sensorimotor homunculus the amount of pre- and postcentral cortex given to a body part follows its innervation, not its size; the homunculus's disproportionate body parts (long fingers, large mouth, large tongue) remain broadly valid, although the drawing cannot be taken at face value.

source.authors: Catani M
source.title: A little man of some importance

evidence_location: Section 'Back to the drawing board', paragraph beginning 'Clearly, the homunculus cannot be taken at face value' (PMC5841206 full text)
quote: the amount of pre- and postcentral cortex dedicated to a body part is not proportional to its size but to the degree of innervation
notes: Same paragraph: 'its most arresting feature of disproportionate body parts remains intriguing and largely valid to this day' and 'With its long fingers, large mouth, and lumbering tongue, the homunculus has made a long-lasting impression.' Qualitative only: the text gives no cm² values; Fig. 2B (areas of the surface maps per body part, re-derived from Penfield and Boldrey's data) was not read numerically.

claim: Penfield and Boldrey scaled their 1937 homunculus by the vertical length of each body part's stimulation map along the pericentral cortex, not by cortical area; textbooks later read its proportions as areas. By surface area the arm's representation is much larger and closer to the hand's, and the first homunculus exaggerated the tongue.

source.authors: Catani M
source.title: A little man of some importance

evidence_location: Section 'Back to the drawing board': paragraph on Leyton and Sherrington, and paragraph comparing the redrawn homunculi (Fig. 4)
quote: Penfield and Boldrey made the controversial choice of using the vertical length along the pericentral cortex (Fig. 2D) to scale their homunculus.
notes: Next sentence: 'Somehow this information went missing when reproductions of the homunculus started to appear in popular textbooks, where its altered proportions were thought to reflect the extension of the area of each body part (Fig. 2B).' Later: 'the size of the tongue was clearly exaggerated in the first homunculus' and 'when using the surface area, the representation of the arm is much larger and closer to that of the hand and fingers.' Consequence for the site: patch sizes copied from the textbook homunculus would overstate the tongue.

claim: Penfield and Boldrey's map pooled cortical stimulation in 126 awake patients operated under local anaesthesia between 1928 and 1936; their data show a clear degree of overlap between the stimulation fields of different body parts, not an orderly sequence of separate areas.

source.authors: Catani M
source.title: A little man of some importance

evidence_location: Opening section (before the heading 'What is the homunculus made of?'); section 'Back to the drawing board' (Fig. 3, overlap maps)
quote: a clear degree of functional overlap between stimulation fields rather than an orderly sequence of segregated areas as their homunculus suggests
notes: Opening section: 'data sourced from the cortical stimulation of 126 patients, who were operated under local anaesthesia by Penfield between 1928 and 1936'. 'Back to the drawing board': 'These maps indicate a high degree of overlay between different body parts, especially in the proximity of the central sulcus.' Relevance: functional areas are not cleanly separated discs.

claim: Primary source of the homunculus: Penfield and Boldrey (1937) drew it as a visualization of the order and comparative size of body parts on the Rolandic (central) cortex, from electrical stimulation in awake patients.

source.authors: Penfield W, Boldrey E
source.title: Somatic motor and sensory representation in the cerebral cortex of man as studied by electrical stimulation

evidence_location: Legend of the homunculus figure, seen only as quoted by Catani 2017, section 'Back to the drawing board'. The original was not opened: the publisher page offers only a paywalled PDF.
quote: a visualization of the order and comparative size of the parts of the body as they appear from above down upon the Rolandic cortex
notes: Secondhand quotation (Catani 2017, t9-01 to t9-03). Cite Catani for any statement about the homunculus; the original pages were not seen. Claim motor-map already dropped Penfield and Boldrey for the same reason. Catani also quotes Penfield and Rasmussen (1950): such drawings 'may easily become confusing if too much significance is attributed to the shape and comparative size'.

claim: Direct electrical stimulation of the precentral gyrus in 100 awake patients (248 motor-positive sites) found two main zones, hand and face/tongue, whose cortex is proportionally much larger than their body volume; the tongue's representation is at least as large as the hand's.

source.authors: Roux FE, Niare M, Charni S, Giussani C, Durand JB
source.title: Functional architecture of the motor homunculus detected by electrostimulation

evidence_location: Discussion, third point (paragraph beginning 'Thirdly, although we detected many types of movements'); accepted author manuscript
quote: The hand and the face/mouth areas occupied parts of the cortex that were proportionally much larger than their body volume.
notes: Next sentence: 'The human cortical representation of the tongue occupies an area at least as large as that of the hand.' Results: 'Localizations were slightly more variable for the face, lips, and tongue areas, a rather large region in the motor homunculus.' Positive sites per body part (Table 2): foot 4, knee 1, hip 4; fingers 49, thumb 11, single fingers 11; wrist 24; lip 38; tongue 35; jaw 12; larynx 14. Counts reflect which cortex was exposed in surgery (the medial leg area is rarely exposed), so they are not area measurements. Read from the authors' accepted manuscript (not copy-edited); volume and pages from the Europe PMC record.

claim: Single stimulation sites that evoke a movement in human primary motor cortex are very small, about 3 mm x 3 mm (often < 10 mm²), and one movement can be evoked from several separate sites. At this scale a functional site is roughly 70 to 110 times smaller than the 6 to 10 cm² of synchronous cortex needed for a scalp potential.
units: mm² per motor-positive site (about 3 mm x 3 mm)

source.authors: Roux FE, Niare M, Charni S, Giussani C, Durand JB
source.title: Functional architecture of the motor homunculus detected by electrostimulation

evidence_location: Results, first paragraph; Abstract ('very small (often <10 mm2) areas'); Discussion, first point
quote: The motor positive areas were located in very small patches of cortex (approximately 3 mm x 3 mm - Fig. 1).
notes: Discussion: 'First, the contralateral movements of the body are represented in small patches of cortex.' and 'individual movements could be induced by multiples sites'. Site size is a property of stimulation mapping, not the total size of a body-part representation. The 70 to 110 times ratio is this file's arithmetic (6 to 10 cm² divided by 0.09 cm²).

claim: Functional MRI of touch on eight body sites in six adults: the primary somatosensory cortex area responding to one middle fingertip was (12 ± 5) cm², nearly 25% of the postcentral gyrus and sulcus, while the largest foot cluster per subject was 7.8 to 200 mm² and the largest forehead (glabella) cluster 10 to 74 mm².
units: cm² of S1 responding to one fingertip (mean; range field is ± 1 SD)

source.authors: Willoughby WR, Thoenes K, Bolding M
source.title: Somatotopic arrangement of the human primary somatosensory cortex derived from functional magnetic resonance imaging

evidence_location: Results 3.2 'Individual Somatosensory Maps' (paragraph on cortical magnification factors) and Table 1 (cluster areas, mm²); Discussion 4.3 'Large Variability of Somatosensory Cortical Magnification'
quote: The cortical surface area for this skin region was found to be (12 ± 5) cm2.
notes: Section 4.3: 'the finger representation was on the order of 10 cm2, nearly 25% of the total surface area of the postcentral gyrus and sulcus', but 'for participant D, the surface area was only 3 cm2'. Largest cluster per subject read from Table 1: finger 335 to 1340 mm², foot 7.8 to 200 mm², forehead 10.1 to 73.9 mm²; within each subject the fingertip cluster is 3 to over 100 times the foot cluster. Each stimulator touched about 4 cm² of skin. Caveats: six subjects, BOLD area depends on the correlation threshold (ρ ≥ 0.45), the table sums (3.4 to 13.4 cm²) do not exactly match the text's 12 ± 5 cm², and this is S1 touch, not motor cortex. No accessible source gave a comparable cm² measure for motor cortex (M1).

claim: Precision fMRI shows separate effector-specific foot, hand and mouth regions in primary motor cortex, but the classic continuous homunculus is interrupted by inter-effector regions (the somato-cognitive action network) with distinct connectivity, structure and function.

source.authors: Gordon EM, Chauvin RJ, Van AN, et al.
source.title: A somato-cognitive action network alternates with effector regions in motor cortex

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 37076628)
quote: we find that the classic homunculus is interrupted by regions with distinct connectivity, structure and function, alternating with effector-specific (foot, hand and mouth) areas
notes: Supports distinct foot, hand and mouth 'functional patches' in M1 while showing they are not one continuous strip. Only the abstract was read; no areas in cm² are taken from this paper.

claim: With simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG in 16 temporal-lobe-epilepsy patients (about 600 interictal spikes), cortical spikes of < 6 cm² were never seen on the scalp, only 10% of those < 10 cm² were, 90% of those > 10 cm² were, and synchronous activation of 10 to 20 cm² of gyral cortex was common.

source.authors: Tao JX, Ray A, Hawes-Ebersole S, Ebersole JS
source.title: Intracranial EEG substrates of scalp EEG interictal spikes

evidence_location: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (Europe PMC record, PMID 15857432)
quote: Intracranial spikes with <6 cm(2) of area were never associated with scalp EEG spikes.
notes: Also: '90% of cortical spikes with a source area of >10 cm(2) produced scalp EEG spikes, whereas only 10% of cortical spikes having <10 cm(2) of source area produced scalp potentials' and 'Synchronous or at least temporally overlapping activation of 10-20 cm(2) of gyral cortex is common.' Area was estimated from the number of intracranial contacts with concurrent depolarization. These are pathological (epileptic) events, not functional areas: a synchronous patch need not be a functional patch. Same source as claim tao-area.

claim: Clinical rule of thumb for spontaneous EEG: something like 6 to 10 cm² of contiguous cortex (about 200 to 300 macrocolumns) must be synchronously active to be recorded at the scalp; the estimate does not necessarily apply to averaged evoked or event-related potentials.

source.authors: Nunez PL, Nunez MD, Srinivasan R
source.title: Multi-scale neural sources of EEG: genuine, equivalent, and representative. A tutorial review

evidence_location: Section 'Effects of Volume Conduction', p. 202 (published version, eScholarship copy, CC BY)
quote: something like 6–10 cm2 of contiguous tissue (about 200–300 macrocolumns) must be synchronously active to be recorded as EEG
notes: Cited there to Delucchi et al. 1962, Cooper et al. 1965, Ebersole 1997, Nunez and Srinivasan 2006, Schomer and Lopes da Silva 2018. Next sentence: 'These estimates do not necessarily apply when scalp data are averaged over multiple trials in evoked (EP) or event related potentials (ERP).' The bioRxiv v2 preprint says '(about 300 macrocolumns)'. Topic-3 entry t3-25 quotes 'about 6 to 10 cm2 of contiguous, synchronously active tissue', which matches neither version word for word.

claim: Each scalp EEG electrode reflects synaptic source activity in something like 10 to 50 cm² of the cortical sheet (about 10^3 to 10^4 mm³ of tissue, 100 million to a billion neurons).
units: cm² of cortex seen by one scalp electrode

source.authors: Nunez PL, Nunez MD, Srinivasan R
source.title: Multi-scale neural sources of EEG: genuine, equivalent, and representative. A tutorial review

evidence_location: Section 'Multi-Scale Source Estimates', bullet 'Macro scale fields', p. 194 (published version)
quote: each electrode reflects synaptic source activity occurring within large parts of the underlying brain, something like 10 to 50 cm2 of the cortical sheet
notes: Continues with cortical tissue volumes of approximately 10^3 to 10^4 mm³ (paraphrased: the exponents are superscripts in the PDF) and 'EEG typically represents the space-averaged source activity in tissue containing on the order of 100 million to a billion neurons.'

claim: The scalp EEG recorded by one electrode is a spatiotemporally smoothed version of the local field potential integrated over 10 cm² or more of cortex.

source.authors: Buzsáki G, Anastassiou CA, Koch C
source.title: The origin of extracellular fields and currents: EEG, ECoG, LFP and spikes

evidence_location: Box 1, 'Electroencephalography' paragraph (PMC4907333 author manuscript)
quote: a spatiotemporally smoothed version of the local field potential (LFP), integrated over an area of 10 cm2 or more
notes: Same source as claim area-rule (buzsaki2012). Gives no primary measurement; consistent with t9-09 and t9-10.

claim: Cooper, Winter, Crow and Walter (1965), with chronically implanted subcortical, cortical and scalp electrodes in humans, are cited as an original source of the roughly 6 cm² synchronous-cortex rule of thumb.

source.authors: Cooper R, Winter AL, Crow HJ, Walter WG
source.title: Comparison of subcortical, cortical and scalp activity using chronically indwelling electrodes in man

evidence_location: Not verifiable: the Europe PMC record (PMID 14255050) has no abstract and the full text is paywalled
notes: Only the bibliographic record was seen. Nunez et al. 2019 (t9-10) cite it, together with Delucchi 1962 and Ebersole 1997, for the 6 to 10 cm² rule. Use Tao 2005 (t9-09) as the primary measurement.

claim: In a detailed finite-element head model checked against scalp EEG, scalp amplitude grew almost linearly with the cortical extent of a synchronous generator, but moving a generator of fixed extent to another cortical location changed the scalp amplitude by factors greater than 3.
units: factor of scalp-amplitude change with location at fixed generator extent (lower bound)

source.authors: von Ellenrieder N, Beltrachini L, Perucca P, Gotman J
source.title: Size of cortical generators of epileptic interictal events and visibility on scalp EEG

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 24636878)
quote: We observed an almost linear relationship between the amplitude of scalp electric potential and the extent of the generator on the cortex.
notes: Continues: 'However, this relationship is subject to substantial variability, with variations in factors greater than 3 occurring simply by changing the location on the cortex of generators of fixed extent.' Model with 8 million elements and 8 tissues. Implication: patch area alone does not fix visibility; location and orientation matter (for example the foot area in the interhemispheric fissure).

claim: Scalp fast oscillations in the 80 to 200 Hz ripple band, more than 10 times smaller than interictal spikes on the scalp, are consistent with cortical generators of only about 1 cm², because the scalp background falls steeply with frequency; the 6 to 10 cm² rule is not a hard floor for every band.
units: cm² (generator extent consistent with scalp fast oscillations)

source.authors: von Ellenrieder N, Beltrachini L, Perucca P, Gotman J
source.title: Size of cortical generators of epileptic interictal events and visibility on scalp EEG

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 24636878)
quote: their median amplitude on scalp EEG recordings is more than 10 times smaller than IEDs and consistent with cortical generators of approximately 1 cm(2)
notes: Background power in scalp EEG is 'inversely proportional to a power of 2.5 of the frequency'. Epileptic high-frequency oscillations in patients, not motor rhythms; the 1 cm² is model-based. IEDs = interictal epileptiform discharges.

claim: The reactive sources of the magnetic mu rhythm (10 and 20 Hz components, suppressed by thumb movement) cluster on partly overlapping cortical areas 6 to 8 cm² wide along the central sulcus: 10 Hz mainly at the primary somatosensory hand cortex, 20 Hz slightly more anterior.
units: cm² (source area of the hand-area mu rhythm)

source.authors: Salmelin R, Hari R
source.title: Spatiotemporal characteristics of sensorimotor neuromagnetic rhythms related to thumb movement

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 8072694)
quote: they clustered on partly overlapping cortical areas of 6-8 cm2 wide along the course of the central sulcus
notes: Four subjects, 24-channel magnetometer (MEG), thumb movements. Abstract: 'The 10-Hz rhythmic oscillations occurred predominantly at the primary somatosensory hand cortex; the sources of the 20-Hz signals were slightly more anterior.' The synchronous patch of this physiological rhythm is about the size of the scalp-visibility threshold (t9-09, t9-10), and the two rhythms of one body region have different, partly overlapping generators. Value 7 is the midpoint chosen here.

claim: With subdural grids in 9 patients, a 7 to 11 Hz mu rhythm appeared over stimulation-mapped sensorimotor cortex (5 to 16 electrodes per patient) and was blocked by movement of the body part represented at that site: presence and blocking of mu are specific to the local somatic representation.

source.authors: Arroyo S, Lesser RP, Gordon B, Uematsu S, Jackson D, Webber R
source.title: Functional significance of the mu rhythm of human cortex: an electrophysiologic study with subdural electrodes

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 7691544)
quote: We conclude that both the presence and blocking of mu rhythm are specific to the somatic representation of the cortex from which it is recorded.
notes: Also: 'There was correspondence between the body area movement of which blocked the mu at a given site and the body region that was affected by stimulation at the same site.' Best evidence that, at electrocorticography (ECoG) scale, synchronous rhythm and functional area line up. Fronto-temporal grids: face and arm cortex, not the foot area.

claim: The movement-related suppression and rebound of the about 20 Hz rhythm follow the motor representation of fingers, toes and mouth, whereas the about 10 Hz rhythm has a stable origin near the hand somatosensory cortex whatever moves.

source.authors: Salmelin R, Hämäläinen M, Kajola M, Hari R
source.title: Functional segregation of movement-related rhythmic activity in the human brain

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 9343608)
quote: rebound of the 20-Hz rhythm followed, along the motor cortex, the representation of fingers, toes, and mouth
notes: Continues: 'as opposed to the stable origin of the 10-Hz rhythms close to the hand somatosensory cortex.' Opening sentence: 'Multiple synaptic interconnections in the human brain support concerted rhythmic activity of a large number of cortical neurons, typically close to 10 and 20 Hz.' MEG. So synchronous patches align with functional areas for the 20 Hz rhythm but not for the 10 Hz mu.

claim: Scalp EEG desynchronization (ERD) appears over the primary hand area during finger movement and over the primary foot area during toe movement; the hand effect was seen in every subject, the foot effect was harder to find.

source.authors: Pfurtscheller G, Neuper C, Andrew C, Edlinger G
source.title: Foot and hand area mu rhythms

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 9202999)
quote: ERD was found over the primary hand area during finger movement and over the primary foot area during toe movement.
notes: Continues: 'The former was observed in every subject, the latter was more difficult to find. From these results it can be speculated that each primary sensorimotor area has its own intrinsic rhythm, which becomes desynchronized when the corresponding area is activated.' The per-area rhythm is the authors' speculation. ERD = event-related desynchronization.

claim: Alpha and lower-beta desynchronization (ERD) marks activated sensorimotor cortex and synchronization (ERS) marks resting or idling cortex: the hand-area mu rhythm grows during foot movement or visual processing, when the hand area is not needed.

source.authors: Pfurtscheller G, Neuper C, Andrew C, Edlinger G
source.title: Foot and hand area mu rhythms

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 9202999)
quote: event-related synchronization (ERS) in the same frequency bands can be seen as an electrophysiological correlate of resting or idling cortical areas
notes: Preceding sentence: 'Event-related desynchronization (ERD) of rhythms within alpha and lower beta bands is characteristic of activated cortical areas ready to process information or to prepare a movement'. Also: 'ERS, in the form of an enhanced mu rhythm on electrodes overlying the primary hand area, was observed not only during visual processing but also during foot movement.' Key for the subtitle: an area is most synchronous when idle; using it reduces its synchrony, so functional use does not 'create' the synchronous event.

claim: With 60 EEG electrodes in nine subjects, imagining hand movement blocked the hand-area mu rhythm in all subjects, while imagining foot or tongue movement enhanced the hand-area mu rhythm in most; desynchronized components centred at 10.9 ± 0.9 Hz, synchronized ones at 12.0 ± 1.0 Hz.

source.authors: Pfurtscheller G, Brunner C, Schlögl A, Lopes da Silva FH
source.title: Mu rhythm (de)synchronization and EEG single-trial classification of different motor imagery tasks

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 16443377)
quote: an enhancement of the hand area mu rhythm was observed during foot or tongue motor imagery in the majority of the subjects
notes: Also: 'During hand motor imagery, the hand mu rhythm blocked or desynchronized in all subjects'. On the scalp, foot and tongue imagery showed up largely as synchrony rising over the hand area, not as a visible foot or tongue patch. Already a site reference (pfurtscheller2006).

claim: Event-related desynchronization and synchronization are highly frequency-band specific, and the same or different scalp locations can show them at the same time.

source.authors: Pfurtscheller G, Lopes da Silva FH
source.title: Event-related EEG/MEG synchronization and desynchronization: basic principles

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 10576479)
quote: either the same or different locations on the scalp can display ERD and ERS simultaneously
notes: Abstract also: 'the ERD/ERS is highly frequency band-specific'. Full text (with its focal ERD / surround ERS discussion) not opened.

claim: Electrocorticography in five patients making tongue, fist and foot contractions: early alpha desynchronization was spatially diffuse and not somatotopically specific, spreading beyond functional-anatomical boundaries; beta desynchronization was often more discrete and somatotopic; body-part representations overlap more than previously thought.

source.authors: Crone NE, Miglioretti DL, Gordon B, Sieracki JM, Wilson MT, Uematsu S, Lesser RP
source.title: Functional mapping of human sensorimotor cortex with electrocorticographic spectral analysis. I. Alpha and beta event-related desynchronization

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 9874480)
quote: alpha ERD commonly occurred in a diffuse spatial pattern that was not somatotopically specific
notes: Also: 'The topography of beta ERD was often more discrete and somatotopically specific than that of alpha ERD'; 'The topographical spread of alpha ERD beyond expected functional-anatomical boundaries'; 'We agree with others that the somatotopic representations of different body parts overlap more than previously thought.' Late-phase alpha ERD became more focused. Evidence that synchronous patches can span beyond functional areas.

claim: Electrocorticography in 22 subjects: with movement, 8 to 32 Hz power consistently fell and 76 to 100 Hz power rose, and the high-frequency changes were more focal than the low-frequency ones; maps were somatotopic and followed the classic homunculus.

source.authors: Miller KJ, Leuthardt EC, Schalk G, Rao RP, Anderson NR, Moran DW, Miller JW, Ojemann JG
source.title: Spectral changes in cortical surface potentials during motor movement

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 17329441)
quote: The power in relevant electrodes consistently decreased in the LFB with movement, whereas the power in the HFB consistently increased.
notes: Also: 'In addition, the HFB changes were more focal than the LFB changes.' LFB = low-frequency band (8-32 Hz), HFB = high-frequency band (76-100 Hz). The rhythms scalp EEG can see (LFB) are the spatially broader ones and they decrease with use.

claim: The blink potential comes from the eyelid moving over the positively charged cornea of an intact eye, which alters the electrical field around the globe; it occurs without eye rotation, and its polarity is opposite to that of a vertical eye rotation in the same direction.

source.authors: Matsuo F, Peters JF, Reilly EL
source.title: Electrical phenomena associated with movements of the eyelid

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 50174)
quote: moving the eyelid over the positively charged cornea of an intact ocular globe alters the electrical field around the globe
notes: Observations on a normal subject, a subject with a non-metallic eye prosthesis and one with unilateral facial paralysis. Abstract: 'The potential occurs in the absence of ocular rotation.' Plöchl et al. 2012 (t9-29) report from this paper that lid movement over a non-metallic prosthetic eye gives no blink potential. Full text paywalled; no amplitudes seen.

claim: With magnetic search coils on eyes and lids (two subjects), spontaneous and forced blinks both produced positive bifrontal EEG potentials maximal at Fp1 and Fp2, and eyelid movement contributed more to them than the upward eye rotation of Bell's phenomenon.

source.authors: Iwasaki M, Kellinghaus C, Alexopoulos AV, Burgess RC, Kumar AN, Han YH, Lüders HO, Leigh RJ
source.title: Effects of eyelid closure, blinks, and eye movements on the electroencephalogram

evidence_location: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (Europe PMC record, PMID 15792897)
quote: both types of blinks caused positive EEG potentials with bifrontal distribution maximum at Fp1 and Fp2
notes: Conclusions: 'our findings indicate that movements of the eyelid contribute to a greater extent to these EEG potentials than do upward eyeball rotations.' Results: 'Spontaneous blinks produced small eye movements directed down and inward'. Only two subjects; no microvolt values or EMG findings in the abstract; full text paywalled (not opened). Some teaching pages still attribute the blink deflection to Bell's phenomenon; this paper contradicts that.

claim: The cornea sits at a steady potential of about +13 mV relative to the forehead, and blink potentials are caused by the eyelids sliding down over this positively charged cornea.

source.authors: Lins OG, Picton TW, Berg P, Scherg M
source.title: Ocular artifacts in EEG and event-related potentials. I: Scalp topography

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 8260327)
quote: The cornea shows a steady DC potential of approximately +13 mV relative to the forehead.
notes: Next sentence: 'Blink potentials are caused by the eyelids sliding down over the positively charged cornea.' Also: 'Propagation factors for blinks and upward eye-movements are significantly different.' DC = direct current (steady) potential.

claim: In 60 subjects, blinks and upward saccades produced very different scalp topographies, explained by different generators: eyelids sliding over the positively charged cornea for blinks, rotation of the corneoretinal dipole for saccades.

source.authors: Picton TW, van Roon P, Armilio ML, Berg P, Ille N, Scherg M
source.title: The correction of ocular artifacts: a topographic perspective

evidence_location: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (Europe PMC record, PMID 10656511)
quote: Blink potentials are caused by the eyelids sliding down over the positively charged cornea, whereas saccade potentials are caused by changes in the orientation
notes: Sentence ends 'of the corneoretinal dipole.' Results: 'Blinks and upward saccades generated potentials with very different topographies.'

claim: During a blink the lid slides over the cornea, which is positive relative to the forehead, and acts as a sliding electrode that short-circuits the cornea to the scalp; blink artifacts are mostly frontal, voluntary blinks are longer and larger than spontaneous ones, and lid movement over a prosthetic eye gives no blink potential.

source.authors: Plöchl M, Ossandón JP, König P
source.title: Combining EEG and eye tracking: identification, characterization, and correction of eye movement artifacts in electroencephalographic data

evidence_location: Results, 'Eyelid-induced artifacts' (first paragraph) and Fig. 5 legend; Discussion, 'Eyelid artifacts'
quote: Thereby the lid acts like a “sliding electrode,” short-circuiting the cornea to the scalp and producing artifacts in the EEG signal
notes: Preceding sentence: 'During blinking the eyelid slides down over the cornea, which is positively charged with respect to the forehead.' Also: 'Blink artifacts are easy to identify even in raw data and show a topographic distribution mostly over frontal electrodes.' Fig. 5 legend: 'Voluntary blinks are of longer duration and result in higher amplitudes than involuntary blinks.' Discussion: 'Active or passive movements over a non-metallic prosthetic eye do not result in blinking potentials (Matsuo et al., 1975).' Blink-associated eye movements 'only play a minor role'. No muscle (EMG) component of blinks is described.

claim: Uncorrected blinks are typically 100 to 200 µV in the frontal channels.

source.authors: Luck SJ
source.title: Applied Event-Related Potential Data Analysis (open textbook), Chapter 8 'Artifact Detection and Rejection'

evidence_location: §8.3, paragraph on artifact correction
quote: 1-2 µV in the frontal channels (because uncorrected blinks are typically 100-200 µV in these channels)
notes: Textbook statement with no primary citation; same source as claim blink-amplitude (luck2022). Agrees with the measured values in t9-31. Value 150 is the midpoint.

claim: In 31 subjects (62-channel EEG, right-mastoid reference), the blink peak at FP1 averaged about 160 µV (subject means 84 to 306 µV, SD across subjects 62.5 µV), against about 30 µV for other EEG; mean blink width at FP1 was 0.197 s (subject means 0.099 to 0.279 s).
units: µV (blink peak at FP1, mean of subject means)

source.authors: Guttmann-Flury E, Sheng X, Zhu X
source.title: Dataset combining EEG, eye-tracking, and high-speed video for ocular activity analysis across BCI paradigms

evidence_location: Methods, 'A priori sample size estimation'; Technical Validation, 'Blinks', Table 3 (rows 'Mean' 160.1 ± 56.4 µV and 'SD' 62.5; column 'Blink width on FP1', mean 0.197 s)
quote: With blink potentials averaging at 160 ± 50 μV, significantly higher than other EEG data averaging at 30 ± 20 μV
notes: Ground electrode on the forehead; the paper does not define 'blink width'; Fig. 6 blink traces were low-pass filtered at 10 Hz. Eyelid EMG electrodes were also recorded, and the text reports that frontopolar EEG, EOG and the eyelid 'electromyogram (EMG) sensors ... record similar patterns', i.e. the slow lid potential dominates even there; no EMG burst values are given. Site note: section 5 shows blinks '160 ms wide', a width not given by its cited claims (blink-amplitude, blink-rate); this paper's subject means (99 to 279 ms) bracket it.

claim: In whole-head MEG of voluntary blinks (8 adults), fronto-temporal sensors showed a slow wave lasting about 400 ms plus a small burst above 30 Hz at blink onset; the authors attribute the anterior activity likely to muscle contraction plus eyelid currents. This is the closest published evidence of a blink muscle burst outside the head, but it is MEG, not EEG, and gives no amplitude.
units: Hz (lower edge of the burst's frequency content)

source.authors: Bardouille T, Picton TW, Ross B
source.title: Correlates of eye blinking as determined by synthetic aperture magnetometry

evidence_location: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (Europe PMC record, PMID 16564205)
quote: a small burst of activity with frequencies above 30 Hz at the initiation of the blink
notes: Abstract: 'Fronto-temporal MEG sensors showed a large slow wave lasting approximately 400 ms'; group maps of 32-64 Hz activity increased 'in and around the orbits'; 'The anterior activation is likely a combination of muscle contraction and eyelid currents.' The abstract does not name the orbicularis oculi. Full text paywalled (not opened), so burst amplitude and duration are unknown. No source found states an orbicularis oculi EMG burst's amplitude, frequency content, duration or electrodes in scalp EEG.

claim: Of four proposed mechanisms for blink potentials (eye rotation during the blink, lid-induced resistance changes, EMG of lid and eyeball muscles, neural activity), the EMG contribution is described only as possibly detectable, citing the MEG study of Bardouille et al. 2006.

source.authors: Ball T, Kern M, Mutschler I, Aertsen A, Schulze-Bonhage A
source.title: Signal quality of simultaneously recorded invasive and non-invasive EEG

claim: The orbicularis oculi EMG of reflex blinks, recorded with electrodes at the eye 12 or 36 mm apart, keeps its true signal power best with an average band of 28 to 500 Hz (12 to 500 Hz for photic blinks).

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record, PMID 9844430)

claim: Blink lid closure is produced by active orbicularis oculi contraction together with passive downward forces, measured with search coils and orbicularis oculi EMG from modified skin electrodes; every blink therefore involves an orbicularis oculi EMG burst at the eye.

claim: Verdict on the proposed section 4 subtitle: partly accurate, reword it. Supported: body-part areas of sensorimotor cortex differ in size (hand and face/tongue large, tongue at least as large as the hand, foot small). Not supported: 'create synchronous events'. The rhythms a person can steer (mu, beta) are strongest when an area is idle and fall when that body part moves or is imagined moving. Synchronous patches only partly match functional areas: 20 Hz follows the body map, 10 Hz sits near the hand area whatever moves, and early alpha suppression spreads past area borders. Representations also overlap rather than forming separate patches. Recommended subtitle: 'Hand, foot and tongue areas differ in size, and each can carry its own rhythm'. Alternative that names the control mechanism: 'Hand, foot and tongue areas differ in size, and moving one quiets its rhythm'.

source.authors: Synthesis of entries t9-01 to t9-24 (this file)
source.title: Fact-check of the proposed subtitle for section 4 ('From outside, patches of cortex blur into broad blobs')

evidence_location: Sizes: t9-01, t9-02, t9-05, t9-06, t9-07. Overlap: t9-03, t9-08, t9-23. Scalp-visible synchrony: t9-09 to t9-16. Alignment of rhythm and area: t9-16 to t9-19, t9-23, t9-24. Synchrony falls with use: t9-19 to t9-21, t9-24.
quote: Cortical areas have functional patches of different sizes that create synchronous events
notes: The quote is the wording under review. (1) 'Functional patches of different sizes': true for body-part representations (t9-01, t9-05, t9-07). But the textbook homunculus is scaled by length along the central sulcus, not area, and exaggerates the tongue (t9-02). Representations overlap (t9-03, t9-23) and are interrupted by inter-effector regions (t9-08). (2) 'Create synchronous events': misleading. Each area can host a rhythm (ECoG: mu specific to the local representation, t9-17; 20 Hz follows fingers, toes and mouth, t9-18; hand and foot area ERD, t9-19). But synchrony is highest when the area idles and drops when it is used (t9-20, t9-21, t9-24), so use removes the event rather than creating it. (3) Functional patch versus synchronous patch: not the same thing. The 10 Hz mu has a stable origin near the hand area for any movement (t9-18); its generators cover 6 to 8 cm² (t9-16); early alpha suppression spreads past functional borders (t9-23); the visible low-frequency changes are broader than the focal high-gamma ones (t9-24). A single stimulation-mapped motor site is about 0.09 cm², roughly 70 to 110 times smaller than the 6 to 10 cm² of synchronous cortex a scalp potential needs (t9-06, t9-09, t9-10). So EEG sees synchrony spanning most of a body-part area, not a small functional patch. Synchronous events also occur with no functional patch behind them, e.g. interictal spikes (t9-09). (4) Figure consistency: section 4 currently gives all five patches one shared radius (state.radiusMm in src/sections/dim-model.ts), so 'differ in size' would contradict the figure unless the radii are made to differ. Sourced sizes for that: S1 fingertip about 12 cm² against foot clusters of at most 2 cm² (t9-07); M1 tongue at least as large as the hand (t9-05). No accessible source gave a cm² area per body part in M1. The recommended subtitle has no abbreviations and no dashes.
